analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "by the state unless there was some cause to disentitle him to those benefits. What are the benefits here? The benefit is created by the state law, the Fair Employment Practices Act, that he be free from discrimination in employment. That is, what would have been otherwise at will here is created for a cause that his employer cannot terminate him or discriminate against him on the basis of his physical handicap. And it provides to him an individual remedy, a remedy that he, if he is discriminated against by his particular employer, can proceed to the Fair Employment Practices Commission and obtain relief. He may obtain reinstatement. He may obtain back pay here amounting to perhaps as high as $15,000. And he may also obtain other relief to eliminate the continuing effects of the discriminatory. Counsel, did the Illinois Court not determine, however, that where the pre-hearing conference is not granted in a timely fashion or conducted in a timely fashion, that in fact he had no right? Isn't that the effect, if you will, of the Illinois Court's state determination, which makes your argument under procedural due process more difficult? It maybe saves your argument on equal protection, but I'm not sure that under those circumstances, you have a procedural due process argument left. Well, here he already had obtained access to the procedures of the Commission by filing a timely charge that set forth sufficient allegations. And then, under the statutory structure set forth in the Fair Employment Practices Act, it's clear that he had an expectancy at that point that he would not be deprived of his opportunity to recover from the company except upon a showing of cause. What if the Supreme Court of Illinois had held that the entire Illinois FEPC violated the Illinois Constitution? Well, we don't contend that Mr. Logan had a right to force the authorities in Illinois to adopt the Fair Employment Practices Act. Nor do we contend that they cannot repeal that act. But we say that when there is a termination of an individual's rights, Mr. Logan's rights, and not by a repeal that affects the whole general public or a general class of the public, that he's entitled to the procedural requirements of due process, and that the decision, the consequence that the Illinois Supreme Court interpreted the failure to hold the timely fact-finding conference is a procedure, because it's a decision that your rights will be terminated without a chance to be heard and without any consideration whatsoever about whether you have been discriminated against or whether you haven't, and whether you should win or the company should win. Well, Mr. Palmer, what is it he was denied the fact-finding hearing in respect? The right to have a statutory hearing within 120 days, or are you saying, no, it's more than that? It's the right to pursue the basic underlying claim. Which is it? It's the second. The second. I mean, he also lost the first by definition, but our complaint is that the result of losing the fact-finding conference, as determined by the Illinois Supreme Court, is he loses all his rights. That's just about a procedural due process. That's correct. And he loses his job for what he claims was a bad reason. That's correct. And he loses his chance to recover. Like you say, it's the same thing as saying you can't be fired except for cause. That's correct. And he's saying you couldn't be fired for X cause. Well, the state of Illinois... Says he can't. That's right. They say that he can't be fired if it amounts to a discrimination because of physical handicap. And that right substantive entitlement with respect to his employment created by the Fair Employment Practices Act is necessarily protected, as is any other property interest, only by the state's coercive power to enforce it, which is through the cause of action, which is given to him to proceed to the Fair Employment Practices Commission to file a charge if he missed... I think it's your argument would be the same if they didn't provide the hearing at all. Oh, yes. Having created the four-cause entitlement in the first case. And that this business of negligently missetting the date is just nails home your argument. Yes. It can be... It's just a... But your basic claim is that once they created the expectation, they had to have a hearing to... Well, some kind of hearing, we don't... Some kind. The failure to have any kind of a hearing is for sure a violation. And we say at the very bottom, the failure to have any kind of decision with respect to whether he should or should not prevail... I gather, Mr. Palm, this is your argument limited to the due process. That's right. And you also have an equal protection claim. That's right. That you didn't get a hearing. A lot of other people get a hearing. That's right. The equal protection claim proceeds on the analysis that there are categories made between those who have a timely fact-finding conference convened by the commission and those who do not. And that it's... There's a special emphasis in the context of this case that the omission is the commission's and no one else. The omission here, as I understand it, was a mistake or something, was it not, on the part of whoever was handling the case for the commission. That's correct, the investigator. The statute says that the commission shall hold a fact-finding conference... This is... I'm not sure I have exactly the words, but this is the context. Shall hold a fact-finding conference within 120 days. It says the commission shall hold... The only obligation put upon Mr. Logan, the complainant in that section of the act, is that he shall attend the fact-finding conference... I want to be clear about this. I gather what your position is on the equal protection that they do for so many within 120 days, and they didn't hear, and therefore denial of equal protection to him. That's right. That's right. In fact, the only Supreme Court opinion, even though we disagree with it in great parts, suggests that everyone should have a fact-finding conference within 120 days. The problem is that, with respect to due process, they've reached an unfair and we think wholly irrational and arbitrary result, should that occurrence not take place. But do you claim that the... On the equal protection issue, do you claim that the deprivation of the hearing was intentional? I thought it was... I thought everybody just thought it might be negligent. No, I'm sorry. Do we claim it's intentional? That the negligent... No, we... That the depriving the deprivation of a hearing is intentional, or do you agree it was only negligent? Well, the record doesn't disclose, but everyone's argued the case, and based upon the information we have... Which is somebody just misread... Mis... Miscalculated the 120 days, and either by misreading a calendar or miscalculating the days... We have no evidence to show an intentional, malicious, or any other kind of motivation. There is a problem here because the action was... The company initiated this particular action as an original action in the Illinois Supreme Court, which has much more limited evidentiary procedures than normal. But no one's put into the record the reason, but we have no reason to believe it wasn't just simple negligence. May I ask, Mr. Palm, would he have a claim, perhaps an Illinois Court of Claims, against either the commission or the investigator? Well, our answer to that is no, it's not at all clear. But we don't think that this court ought to do that. But if he did, I take it he couldn't get reinstatement anyway. That's for sure. He could get only damages, couldn't he? That's correct. He couldn't get reinstatement, and... And he did seek reinstatement, I gather, did he? That's correct. Mm-hmm. With respect to the due process entitlement, I would like to emphasize particular provisions of the Fair Employment Practices Act, which show that his entitlement here to obtain relief against his employer, if his employer discriminated against him, is protected except for a showing of cause. There are significant indicators of the cause requirement. The first is the Section 851 of the Act. The very first section sets forth as public policy purposes, one, to protect individual employees covered by the Act from employment discrimination because of physical handicap, and two, and this is important as well, to protect all employers from unfounded claims of employment discrimination. Second, another indicator is that the Fair Employment Practices Act sets forth a substantive definition to be used in determining cause. It defines in its terms and is in the statute and is interpreted by the courts of Illinois what is an unfair employment practice. And third, this standard of what is an unfair employment practice is also to be measured by an evidentiary test, two different tests at two different times in the proceeding. First, during the investigative stage, the test is substantial evidence, whether or not there is substantial evidence to establish that an unfair employment practice occurred. This level of evidence, the amount is not particularly significant, but the fact that some level of evidence is used to control the discretion of the Commission in deciding who receives the benefits and who does not indicates that they are controlled for cause. The other standard is the preponderance of the evidence standard, which is to be applied by the Commission after they have found substantial evidence, the complaint is issued, discovery has been conducted, and there is a full public hearing. Then the Commission is charged by the statute to decide whether there is evidence, by a preponderance of the evidence, to establish that the unfair employment practice occurred. The fourth indicator here is that there is review, and then indeed judicial review, of the determination of the Commission. First, the investigator's decision about whether there is or is not substantial evidence is reviewable de novo by the Commission. The, my client or any complainant can, if the investigator rules no substantial evidence to support the charge, can submit new evidence, not previously submitted to the investigator, and can submit arguments that were already submitted or new arguments as well. Should the Commission then again decide that there is no substantial evidence, then the review is available to the Circuit Court of Cook County, through the administrative, in our case Cook County, through the Administrative Review Act, and then if, again, that court should affirm, there's further review to the Illinois Appellate Court as a matter of right, and then, of course, discretionary review by a petition for leave to appeal to the Illinois Supreme Court. All of these reviews and judicial reviews indicate that the for-cause requirements set forth in the statute, which must be established by some quantum of evidence, is then further controlled by the Appellate Courts to make sure that there is indeed a for-cause determination and not an at-will decision. Mr. Palmer, we would agree with you that you should have been given the hearing. What would be the subject of the hearing? What would the inquiry be made? What would the inquiry of the hearing be? Yes. Well, the inquiry of the hearing and the decision must be as to the merits of the case, whether or not an unfair employment practice occurred. Now, as a part of that, there certainly... So this would be as if you had got a timely, within a 120-day hearing? That's correct. All you're saying is they can't deny giving you the same thing, even if it's later than 120 days. That's correct. What if the original papers which you filed or sought to file had never been delivered to the Commission and the time, the outside time limit passed? Where would the responsibility lie for the failure of delivery? Let's assume that you had used the United States mails. The... First of all, this is not... There is no statute of limitations problems here, as you are aware. He filed on time. And he already has access, so he's not seeking access, which we think is a distinction. Conceptually, I have a bit of a difficulty with the statute of limitations problem, but I think either way it works out. It doesn't fall within the heart of our case, and that our case can be decided without regard to that. First, to answer directly your question, if one looks at the limitations provision as a substantive... I'm sorry, as a procedural requirement, then it would have to be examined by the procedural requirements of due process. Here, since the burden was on him, to make sure that the papers arrived at the Commission on time, that, in my view, would be adequate under due process. He'd be out then. He would be out, but it was his responsibility, and that's the reason that he should bear the blame, is because it was his responsibility to get those papers to the Commission on time. Here, he had no responsibility to convene the fact-finding conference on time. That was the investigator's responsibility. And... And as a matter, I take it that the Commission itself actually thought the time limits were just discretionary. That's correct. The procedural posture of this case is that the investigator and her supervisor at the Commission denied the company's motion to dismiss the charge on the grounds of the failure to convene the fact-finding conference on time. And the Commission was prepared to go ahead, at which point the original action was brought in the Illinois Supreme Court, and there, the Attorney General, on behalf of the Commission, argued that the... as we did, as a matter of state statutory construction, that the consequence doesn't follow, and it's a... there's a whole other range of... So it might have been reasonable for the claimant to... think that the... think that the 180 days wasn't binding either. Or... No, no, the 180 days says he shall file the charge... Well, I know, but... Yeah, but... What's the... What's the... You mean the fact-finding? 120. 120. So he wouldn't... He might think that the... that the hearing was set beyond 125 days didn't... wasn't crucial at all. That's correct. And the notice that was sent him didn't indicate... Any... Any defect in anything? No, it said you have to appear at the given date. It didn't say, check your calendar to see if this was in 120 days. And had notice... Even if he knew what the statute said, he... He wouldn't necessarily conclude that it was crucial. He wouldn't know from that... What the consequences would be of the failure to have it on time. And on the statute itself... I'm sorry, on the notice itself, it did convey the requirement that he appear at that date or his charge might be dismissed, which he did and he was prepared to proceed. The other... aspect of the... of the problem I have with statute of limitations, to complete my answer... here, is that... it also can be seen really as a precondition to... as... as access has been seen by this Court in other circumstances, that there is a condition to the second half of the entitlement here, which is the use of the coercive powers of the state. And that is that you initiate your action on time, that you pay the filing fee, that you... that you get it there. And... as I say, we don't... either one of these analyses doesn't affect us because our charge was filed on time and the responsibility was directly that of the commission and not of our client to... make sure the conference was held on time. The... Counsel, if in fact you... your client has a cause of action against the state, for example, for negligence, because of what happened, do you... do you have a problem then under the Parrott case and the ensuing case that followed Parrott in holding that a post-deprivation remedy, in effect, will suffice? In... our opinion, Parrott just doesn't apply to this case. This is a case involving procedures and not the... the... like negligent driving or... I mean, this sort of adjudicatory procedures, which just should not be put in the same category as the negligent handling of a hobby kit or the negligent driving of an automobile. Indeed, in the Bonner opinion, Bonner v. Coughlin, written by then Judge Stevens, the analysis of which was adopted in great part in Parrott, was made... clear, absolutely clear, that this analysis was not to apply to procedures because they're at the very heart of the due process requirement. But the... what you want... what was sought in this case was reinstatement. That's right. In any event, it wouldn't be... And you're not going to get that remedy against a state officer. That's correct. That's correct. But I thought the question was whether we were going to get to that. I'm sorry. Well, if you win your case here, what relief do you say you're entitled to? Well, this court should reverse the writ of prohibition that was entered by the only Supreme Court, and we should then go back to the commission, and the investigation should be concluded, and the commission should... the investigators should first decide whether there is substantial evidence that my client was discriminated against by zero and brush company. You want the 120-day hearing now? No, we don't... No, we don't... We've lost that, and there's no way we can have that back within... Well, you want a hearing which would be the one you would have had but for the... That's correct. ...boner of the commission, wouldn't you? That's the kind of hearing you want. That's exactly what it is. What you're really arguing for, I take it, is an equitable concept that that should be done that should have been done. That's correct. And if you win in that hearing, the result is reinstatement. No, no. The result... This would be the substantial evidence. Oh, I know, but what if you win? Overall, we win by propriety evidence? Yes. Mr. Logan will get reinstatement to his job. Yes, that's exactly right. And as well as the other remedies. All you really want is just to go ahead. That's all we want. All Mr. Logan's wanted from the beginning, from the day he filed his charge, five days after he believes he was discriminated, is a chance to prove that. And if he was discriminated against, then he's entitled to the remedies, reinstatement, and the other remedies that are provided. And if he's not, then he loses. And then he has whatever appellate... He does have the appellate remedies provided in Illinois. What's the time lapse here now since the day when you should have had your hearing, as you claim, and the employer could have come in and defended? How much time has elapsed? Oh, hi. How much time has elapsed? The time is... About 18 months. 18 months. Counsel, what if... Is there anything in the Illinois procedure that would provide for mediation at the intermediate stage of the administrative proceeding? Throughout the investigative stage, emphasis is placed upon settlement. And one of the purposes is a fact-finding conference, which is to discuss settlement and the possibility of reaching an accommodation without an adjudication. That's done off the record. Then there is a separate opportunity provided for conciliation before the complaint issues. And if that fails between the parties and both parties... Well, and the complaint particularly has some obligations to be reasonable in the settlement demands, then they issue the complaint and the parties go about discovery and proceed to the hearing. What if this time lag of 18 months, all the fault of the state, not of either of the parties, has impaired the posture of the employer in terms of asserting its position, defending against the claims? That's a problem inherent with any case that's on appeal and reversal is made and you're sent back to follow the right procedures. And I think it's a part of the cost that one has to bear within the system. And the employer here pursued the writ of prohibition. Well, that's correct. After losing out before the commission and the investigator. That's right. There would have been a hearing on the 125th day and there's never been a claim that the five-day period that admittedly ran in any way affected their ability to come forward with evidence or any way to be adequately prepared for the hearing. In effect, what you're saying is that if the employer's posture has been prejudiced, the employer bears a large responsibility for that himself by the way he... That's right. That's right. He caused the prejudice by initiating the action in the Illinois Supreme Court since there was none at the end of the 125th day. Thank you. Mr. Cannell. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. I've never seen Laverne Logan, but I presume that on the day he walked into Zimmerman Brush Company and asked for a job, they recognized that he was a handicapped person. And knowing of that fact, they nevertheless hired him as a probationary employee. They gave him his first job in the shipping room and when they felt he was unable to handle that work, they gave him a second job on a machine where he could sit down. But when they didn't feel he could do that either, they discharged him before the end of the probationary period so that he would not be under the union contract. Logan thought Zimmerman had discriminated against him, but if this alleged discrimination had taken place before 1975 in the state of Illinois, Logan would have no rights at all to sue Zimmerman for anything. In 1975, the Illinois legislature enacted legislation prohibiting employers from discriminating against persons with physical handicaps. That statute did not give Logan an entitlement to sue his private employer under Illinois state law. What it gave him was the right to complain to the State Fair Employment Practices Commission and to tell that commission that he thought that his employer had discriminated against him because of his handicap. Once Logan made that complaint to the State Fair Employment Practices Commission, the issue was left up to the commission and according to Illinois state statutes, that commission was required to do several things. First, it was required to hold a conference within 120 days and that conference served several purposes. One of the major purposes of that conference was that it was for possible conciliation and settlement of Logan's claim. Another reason for the conference was to take some evidence. The statute also provided that there was a 180-day period of time within which the commission had to make a decision whether or not a claim against any employer could go forward. Only after the Fair Employment Commission did both and ruled in Logan's favor did Logan ever have a right to pursue any claim for reinstatement or back pay against his employer. Now, through no fault of Logan's, and I add, through no fault of Zimmerman Brush Company, Logan's case never got past step one. He never had the mandatory 120-day conference. Previous Illinois Supreme Court cases had ruled twice as a matter of state law that the 180-day period of time within which the Fair Employment Practices Commission was required to decide whether or not there was substantial cause for a discrimination charge to go ahead was mandatory. And in the second of the two cases, a consolidated case, Board of Governors and Royal Crown Corporation versus the Commission, one of those cases found that a handicapped person could not go ahead on his claim because the Commission had not acted within the 180 days. But do I understand, Mr. Cannell, that the conference would have been held on the 125th day but for Zimmerman seeking the writ of prohibition in the Supreme Court? The conference would have been held. That's correct, Justice Brenner. Well, then I suppose the prospect, at least there was a prospect for us or not, that the Commission would have completed its work within the 180 days but for the intervention of the prohibition proceeding. Yes, Justice Brenner, but the fact is, and I was not a party to those proceedings at that time, but the fact is, Zimmerman was right as a matter of state law and I think for the court to say, well, it's Zimmerman's fault, they went ahead and they filed a petition for writ of prohibition and so it shouldn't make any difference to Zimmerman if they were wrong in getting that writ of prohibition. The fact is, they were right in getting the writ of prohibition. As a matter of state law, they were correct. The state says, yes, the language in the statute for the 120 days and the 180 day provisions is identical and you were right. But that doesn't answer the federal constitutional questions. No, sir, it does not. It does not. Has the statute been changed since this all took place? The statute has been changed. Now, the 120 day, the whole law is put into the Human Rights Act and the 120 day provision is made discretionary. The 180 day period is still mandatory. The Zimmerman, well, as I said, in the Zimmerman case, when the court finally got to it, it had construed, with his Illinois Supreme Court, was construing language relating to the 120 day hearing, which was exactly the same language that they had construed twice before with reference to the mandatory provision in the 180 day hearing. And it's interesting to note. Isn't this argument that they should have known that the 120 day period was jurisdictional? That's what the Supreme Court said. That's what the Supreme Court of Illinois said. They said, we use the same language in 180 day as in 120 day. We've said twice that that was jurisdictional, and they should know that the 120 day period is also jurisdictional. Of course, your client did know it, but the hearing examiner didn't. Yes, that's correct. But That's what made a case in the new Supreme Court. Well. Because the commission and the, and your client disagreed on that. Well, but that whole Well, isn't that right? That's correct, Justice White. That's correct. But this all gets Is your answer to that in part that they can't confer jurisdiction by agreement? I'm sorry, would you? They couldn't confer jurisdiction where the time had already lapsed. Is that your point? They could have waived jurisdiction. They couldn't have waived. They, well, I said that, but I may be wrong. I don't know whether or not they could have waived yours, Well, even if they couldn't, the question is, should you have known it in advance? Well, I assume that Zimmerman's lawyers at that time knew it, but that doesn't really get done. the commission didn't know. Well, but the, but the Illinois Supreme Court said, Justice White, that the commission should have known. The Illinois Supreme Court said, we've told you twice, on identical language, that the 180-day provision is mandatory, and you should have, by reason of those two cases, known that when we use the same language, when the legislature used the same language in the 120-day provision, that that was also mandatory, and this all gets down to a where do you draw the line argument. The Illinois Supreme Court and the Illinois statute both expressed substantial concerns for the rights of the employer. The provision which Mr. Palm read to you from the Illinois Act says it's also the public policy of Illinois to protect employers and labor organizations against unfounded charges of discrimination, and there's an economic point here, which I think was not properly made in our brief, and which I should make to the court. I don't think that Logan had much of a case on the facts, because he was... We're not concerned about that now. I understand that, but it's important from this point of view, and it's important in judging the reasonableness of this 120-day rule. The fact is, no matter how bad a case is, the case becomes worth more and more money as to the defendant employer the longer it languishes! before some commission, because the longer it languishes before some commission, the more back pay is going to build up, and the more expensive the reinstatement and back pay award will be, and so forth... Am I correct, sir, that if it had not been for the rent of prohibition, they wouldn't pursue it? I presume that that is correct. Why are you arguing about that he brought all his arm? He didn't. But it was the... He didn't, did it? It was the... You didn't. Am I right? That's right. And it was our right to do that under the Illinois law, and it was our right to protect ourselves. Or... Did that give you a right to argue that the other guy was responsible for it? But it... Well, wait a minute. Justice Marshall, when we say the other guy was responsible for it, Zimmerman was not responsible for the delay. It had a right to a hearing within that time. Logan... The writ of prohibition was filed by Zimmerman to enforce a right. To enforce a right. The Illinois Supreme Court said it had. And that by doing that, we delayed no agreement. If you had not done that, it might have been settled. That's possible, but I don't... Certainly, we wouldn't be bothered with it. Well, that was through no fault of mine that the court was bothered with it. But if an award had been entered against Zimmerman by the commission, Zimmerman could have appealed through the Illinois court system on the same basis, could he not? But he would waive a right. Right. But I mean, the delay might have been just... Yeah, that's correct, Justice Franklin. He could have said, and I think probably based on the first brief I filed in this case, and based on my client's change of lawyers and change of attitude, he probably feels it would have been the better thing for him to do economically instead of becoming a cause celeb before the state and now the U.S. Supreme Court. But at that point in time, he listened to his labor lawyer who was representing him, and the labor lawyer said, you're entitled to have the hearing within 120 days. That legislation was enacted for your benefit. It's not your fault that that hearing didn't take place on that time, and you might as well take advantage of it. And if anybody's at fault for failing to set the hearing at that time, it's not Zimmerman and it's not Logan. It's the state official who didn't follow the law of the state of Illinois. On the due process issue, supposing the statute said similar procedure but just said one out of every ten complaints shall be dismissed without any hearing, just arbitrarily at random will dismiss one out of every five or ten. Would that violate any due process right now? I think so. Why? Because it's an arbitrary dismissal? It's an arbitrary Well, if you look to the history of these types of remedial statutes, all you have to do is look to the history of the federal government of the EEOC, which has thousands of these cases sitting around for years at a time, never getting tried, never getting disposed of, and when you look at it in terms of the Illinois laws, the law, and my former argument, which is the more these cases hang around, the more it costs the employer, even in a bad case, if he loses one out of ten bad cases. Well, I suppose they should always file a motion to expedite, go in in 30 days and say you don't have to have the hearing for 120, but we'd like to move it along. But you're not guaranteed that the motion's going to be expedited, that the hearing is going to be expedited, you have no control. Suppose the hearing officer comes back. But your client was conscious of litigation promptly. Knowing that, they could have insisted on a hearing within 120 days, I think we have to presume it would have been granted. Well, I don't think that you can presume that it would have been granted. It might have been granted. You don't know what the state administrator is going to do when the state administrator gets a request. But here doesn't the record show that the error was a miscalculation and the administrator understood the 120 day obligation but didn't realize it was jurisdictional? The record shows no such thing. The record shows only that the hearing examiner set the initial hearing within 125 days. People have argued that she was negligent when she did that. I don't think that there's any evidence in the record that she did it intentionally. It was done. Well, in any event, I think that it would be certainly when you go back to the Illinois state law, that state law is that at least at the time Logan's case was pending, the 120 day hearing was required by state law. For this court to say that that requirement is an unconstitutional deprivation of Logan's rights in this case, it would have to come to the conclusion that that mandate from the Illinois legislature is construed by the Illinois Supreme court is wholly arbitrary or irrational. And I submit to the court, based on my economic argument of the cases becoming worth more and more, costing employers more and more the longer that they hang around in administrative tribunals.
